title: How To Manage Well-Behaved, On-Task Group Work
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that teachers who are currently struggling with disorderly group work have already missed the critical window to fix it correctly, and that the only real solution is teaching group work properly from scratch through a deliberate three-stage process. Stage one focuses on precisely defining expectations, modeling them repeatedly with student volunteers, and having students prove readiness through supervised practice with a low-stakes topic. Stage two shifts to sustained, attentive supervision as the teacher gradually introduces real curricular content and extends session length, only pulling back once students demonstrate consistent independent competence. Stage three, joining a small group directly, is reserved for teachers only after mastery has been proven, and he cautions this should be an opportunity to observe more closely rather than to lead the group and let the rest of the class lose structure. The piece closes by tying successful, enjoyable group work to the same broader principle running through his other work: patient, staged preparation followed by gradually transferring full responsibility to students.
points: Group work must be taught in three deliberate stages rather than explained once and assumed to work; skipping the staged approach rarely succeeds at any grade level.
Stage one requires precisely defining expectations, modeling them repeatedly with volunteers, and having students prove readiness through low-stakes supervised practice.
Stage two extends practice to real curricular content while the teacher observes closely, only pulling back once students show consistent independent competence.
Stage three, working with a small group directly, should only happen after mastery is proven, and it should be for closer observation, not to lead the group and abandon the rest of the class.
Well-taught group work is achievable in any classroom regardless of context, but it depends entirely on the preparation done ahead of time, not improvisation.
quotes: If you’re currently struggling to manage group work, it’s already too late. You’ve missed the boat.
To have well-behaved, on-task groups—so you can work with your own small group if you wish without interruption—it must be taught in three stages.

Have your students circle around you and a few volunteers and show them what you want and what you don’t want. Demonstrate your expectations. Break it into simple steps and provide a handout or steps on an easel to follow.
During this stage, you’re going to ensure your students can perform group work perfectly under your attentive observation . Keep practicing and honing their skills over time.
If you do meet with your own group, it should be an opportunity for you to watch at a closer, deeper level, not for you to lead the group and absolve your students of responsibility.
You must teach what impeccable group work looks like until your vision manifests in front of you, like a scene from a movie you’ve watched over and over.
